course.title: NumPy Mastery
course.subtitle: Complete Numerical Computing Program
course.tagline: Learn NumPy. Master Arrays. Build Data Science Skills.
course.description: NumPy from the first array to linear algebra, broadcasting, memory layout, random simulation and real Data Science workflows. Hinglish explanations, runnable code and ten practice sections per module.
prerequisites: Basic arithmetic and an idea of what a matrix is
outcomes: Create and inspect ndarrays and reason about shape, size, ndim and dtype
Index, slice, reshape and broadcast arrays without Python loops
Use universal functions, aggregation and Boolean masks correctly
Tell a view from a copy and control memory usage
Generate reproducible random data and run Monte Carlo simulations
Solve linear systems and choose stable linear-algebra routines
Read and write numeric data with NPY/NPZ and text files
Handle NaN, infinity and masked arrays in real datasets
Vectorise code and benchmark it honestly
Move arrays between NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib and scikit-learn

modules.title: NumPy Introduction and Fundamentals
modules.goal: Understand what NumPy is, why ndarrays beat Python lists for numeric work, and run your first array program.

topics.title: Create your first array
topics.body: np.array turns a Python list into an ndarray: one typed block of memory that supports vectorised maths, so mean() and shape are properties of the data rather than a loop you write.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(a, a.mean(), a.shape)

topics.title: Vectorised arithmetic
topics.body: An operation between an array and a scalar is applied to every element by compiled code, which is why `a * 2` needs no loop and returns a new array instead of mutating `a`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
print(a * 2)

topics.title: Typed memory, not a Python list
topics.body: Every ndarray has one dtype and a fixed itemsize, so nbytes tells you the real memory it occupies; a Python list stores pointers to separate objects and cannot answer that question.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a.dtype, a.itemsize, a.nbytes)

topics.title: Two arrays combine elementwise
topics.body: Arithmetic between two same-shape arrays pairs position by position, so `a + b` is not concatenation and the result keeps the input shape.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a + b)

topics.title: Indexing starts at zero
topics.body: The first element is index 0 and the last is -1, exactly like a Python list, so the same counting rules carry over before reshape changes anything.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([5, 6, 7])
print(a[0], a[-1])

topics.title: Methods return plain results
topics.body: sum, min and max are methods on the array, so the answer arrives as a Python scalar you can print or compare without converting anything.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([4, 1, 9])
print(a.sum(), a.max(), a.min())

topics.title: Convert back to a Python list
topics.body: tolist() turns an ndarray into nested Python lists, which is the right move when the receiver expects plain lists rather than array printing.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([4, 1, 9])
print(a.tolist())

topics.title: Integers and floats carry different dtypes
topics.body: The dtype is inferred from the values you pass, so `np.array([1, 2])` is integer while `np.array([1.0, 2.0])` is float — one of them can hold 2.5 and the other cannot.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1, 2]).dtype, np.array([1.0, 2.0]).dtype)

topics.title: Add a scalar to every element
topics.body: A scalar is broadcast across the whole array, so one `+` replaces a loop. No Python-level iteration happens.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a + 10)

topics.title: Compare an array with a scalar
topics.body: Comparison returns a boolean array of the same shape. That array is what every filter is built on.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([1, 5, 9]) > 4)

topics.title: A Python loop still works over an array
topics.body: Iterating walks the first axis. It is fine for a handful of values and wrong for a million, where a vectorised expression wins.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

total = 0
for value in np.array([2, 4, 6]):
    total += int(value)
print(total)

topics.title: Every array reports its own type
topics.body: `np.array` always returns an `ndarray`. A Python `list` and an `ndarray` are not interchangeable.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(type(np.array([1, 2])).__name__)

tasks.title: Total without a loop
tasks.statement: Build the array `np.array([4, 8, 15, 16])` and store its total, as an int, in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
values = np.array([4, 8, 15, 16])
result = int(values.sum())
print(result)

tasks.title: Double, then take the first two
tasks.statement: Starting from `np.arange(1, 6)`, multiply every element by 2 and store the first two elements in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = (np.arange(1, 6) * 2)[:2]
print(result)

tasks.title: Count the values above ten
tasks.statement: Count how many elements of `np.array([4, 11, 10, 15, 3])` are greater than 10 and store the count as an int in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([4, 11, 10, 15, 3])
result = int((a > 10).sum())
print(result)

tasks.title: Back to a Python list
tasks.statement: Convert `np.array([1.5, 2.5])` to a plain Python list and store it in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = np.array([1.5, 2.5]).tolist()
print(result)

modules.title: ndarray Fundamentals
modules.goal: Read an array's shape, size, ndim, dtype and axes correctly before writing any operation on it.

topics.title: shape, size and ndim
topics.body: shape is one number per axis, size is the product of those numbers and ndim is how many axes exist — the three answers every shape error is really about.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a.shape, a.size, a.ndim)

topics.title: dtype and itemsize
topics.body: The dtype decides how the bytes are interpreted and itemsize is the bytes per element; together they explain both the values you get and the memory you pay.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a.dtype, a.itemsize)

topics.title: Axis means the direction that is collapsed
topics.body: Reducing along axis 0 collapses rows (one result per column) and axis 1 collapses columns (one result per row); reading the output length tells you which axis was reduced.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.sum(axis=0), a.sum(axis=1))

topics.title: len counts the first axis only
topics.body: len() reports the length of axis 0, not the number of elements, so for a (3, 4) array len is 3 while size is 12.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((3, 4))
print(len(a), a.size)

topics.title: Transpose swaps the shape
topics.body: Transposing reverses the axis order, so a (3, 4) array becomes (4, 3) and every operation that follows reads the new shape.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((3, 4))
print(a.T.shape)

topics.title: Mixed literals promote to float
topics.body: One float in the input is enough to make the whole array float64, because a single dtype has to hold every value.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1, 2.5]).dtype)

topics.title: A zero-dimensional array has no axes
topics.body: `np.array(7)` is a 0-d array: it has one value, ndim 0 and an empty shape tuple, which is how a scalar crosses into array code.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
s = np.array(7)
print(s.ndim, s.shape)

topics.title: Bytes are shape times itemsize
topics.body: nbytes is size multiplied by itemsize, so a float32 array of six elements costs 24 bytes and a float64 one would cost 48.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 3), dtype=np.float32)
print(a.nbytes)

topics.title: ndim counts the axes
topics.body: `ndim` is how many indices you need to reach a single value; `size` is how many values exist in total.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.zeros((2, 3, 4))
print(a.ndim, a.size)

topics.title: Ten zeros are one dimension
topics.body: A one-dimensional array has a trailing comma in its shape. That is a 1-tuple, not a scalar.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.zeros(10).shape)

topics.title: Shape is a tuple you can index
topics.body: `shape` is data, not a method. Read `shape[0]` for rows and `shape[1]` for columns instead of calling it.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.ones((2, 2))
print(a.shape[0], a.shape[1])

topics.title: A matrix of one row still has two axes
topics.body: Wrapping a list in a list adds an axis even when there is only one element in it. Shape `(1, 2)` is a matrix, `(2,)` is a vector.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([[7, 8]]).shape)

modules.title: Array Creation and Initialization
modules.goal: Create arrays with zeros, ones, full, arange, linspace, eye and diag, and pick the right constructor for a dataset.

topics.title: zeros, ones and full
topics.body: These allocate a new array of a given shape and fill it: zeros and ones are the common starting points, full repeats any value and needs the fill value explicitly.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.zeros(3), np.ones((2, 2)), np.full(3, 7))

topics.title: arange and linspace
topics.body: arange builds a range by step (the stop is excluded, like range) while linspace builds a fixed number of evenly spaced points including both ends — the safer choice for float grids.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 10, 2), np.linspace(0, 1, 3))

topics.title: Identity and diagonal matrices
topics.body: eye builds an identity matrix of any shape and diag builds a square matrix from a 1-D vector (or extracts the diagonal from a 2-D one).
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.eye(2), np.diag([1, 2]))

topics.title: zeros_like copies a shape
topics.body: `zeros_like` and `ones_like` take the shape and dtype from an existing array, which is how you allocate an accumulator that lines up with real data.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(np.zeros_like(a), np.ones_like(a, dtype=int))

topics.title: linspace can exclude the endpoint
topics.body: With endpoint=False, linspace still gives you a fixed number of points but stops one step short, which is what periodic sampling needs.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.linspace(0, 1, 4, endpoint=False))

topics.title: arange accepts a fractional step
topics.body: arange happily takes a float step, though repeated float addition can drift; linspace is the safer tool when exact spacing matters.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 1, 0.25))

topics.title: ones can take an integer dtype
topics.body: The default float dtype is a choice, not a rule: pass dtype=int when you want ones that stay integers in later arithmetic.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.ones(3, dtype=int))

topics.title: full repeats any value
topics.body: full allocates a shape and fills every cell with the value you give, so a constant column or a sentinel matrix is one call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.full((2, 2), 3, dtype=int))

topics.title: empty allocates without setting values
topics.body: `np.empty` skips initialisation, so it is faster but holds whatever memory was there. Use it only when you overwrite every element next.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.empty(3)
print(a.shape, a.dtype)

topics.title: identity builds an identity matrix
topics.body: `np.identity(n)` is the square identity: ones on the diagonal, zeros elsewhere. It is the neutral element for matrix multiplication.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.identity(2))

topics.title: arange counts down with a negative step
topics.body: The stop value is excluded in both directions. A negative step reverses the walk through the range.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.arange(5, 0, -1))

topics.title: linspace controls the step you get
topics.body: `linspace(start, stop, n)` includes the endpoint and spaces `n` values evenly, which `arange` with floats cannot promise.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.linspace(0, 1, 5))

learn.title: zeros, ones and full
learn.body: These allocate a new array of a given shape and fill it: zeros and ones are the common starting points, full repeats any value and needs the fill value explicitly.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.zeros(3), np.ones((2, 2)), np.full(3, 7))

learn.title: arange and linspace
learn.body: arange builds a range by step (the stop is excluded, like range) while linspace builds a fixed number of evenly spaced points including both ends — the safer choice for float grids.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 10, 2), np.linspace(0, 1, 3))

learn.title: Identity and diagonal matrices
learn.body: eye builds an identity matrix of any shape and diag builds a square matrix from a 1-D vector (or extracts the diagonal from a 2-D one).
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.eye(2), np.diag([1, 2]))

learn.title: zeros_like copies a shape
learn.body: `zeros_like` and `ones_like` take the shape and dtype from an existing array, which is how you allocate an accumulator that lines up with real data.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(np.zeros_like(a), np.ones_like(a, dtype=int))

learn.title: linspace can exclude the endpoint
learn.body: With endpoint=False, linspace still gives you a fixed number of points but stops one step short, which is what periodic sampling needs.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.linspace(0, 1, 4, endpoint=False))

learn.title: arange accepts a fractional step
learn.body: arange happily takes a float step, though repeated float addition can drift; linspace is the safer tool when exact spacing matters.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 1, 0.25))

learn.title: ones can take an integer dtype
learn.body: The default float dtype is a choice, not a rule: pass dtype=int when you want ones that stay integers in later arithmetic.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.ones(3, dtype=int))

learn.title: full repeats any value
learn.body: full allocates a shape and fills every cell with the value you give, so a constant column or a sentinel matrix is one call.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.full((2, 2), 3, dtype=int))

learn.title: empty allocates without setting values
learn.body: `np.empty` skips initialisation, so it is faster but holds whatever memory was there. Use it only when you overwrite every element next.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.empty(3)
print(a.shape, a.dtype)

learn.title: identity builds an identity matrix
learn.body: `np.identity(n)` is the square identity: ones on the diagonal, zeros elsewhere. It is the neutral element for matrix multiplication.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.identity(2))

learn.title: arange counts down with a negative step
learn.body: The stop value is excluded in both directions. A negative step reverses the walk through the range.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.arange(5, 0, -1))

learn.title: linspace controls the step you get
learn.body: `linspace(start, stop, n)` includes the endpoint and spaces `n` values evenly, which `arange` with floats cannot promise.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.linspace(0, 1, 5))

modules.title: Data Types and Type Conversion
modules.goal: Choose an explicit dtype, convert safely with astype and understand overflow, precision and memory cost.

topics.title: Converting with astype
topics.body: astype returns a NEW array with the requested dtype and truncates floats toward zero, so 1.7 becomes 1; the original array is untouched.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.7, 2.9])
print(a.astype(int))

topics.title: Overflow is silent
topics.body: Integer dtypes wrap around on overflow instead of raising, so uint8 arithmetic can turn a large result into a small one — use a wider dtype when the range is not guaranteed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([250], dtype=np.uint8)
print(a + 10)

topics.title: Smaller dtype, smaller memory
topics.body: float32 uses four bytes per element against eight for float64; choosing it deliberately cuts memory and bandwidth in half, at the cost of precision.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=np.float32)
print(a.dtype, a.nbytes)

topics.title: astype truncates toward zero
topics.body: Casting float to int does not round: it drops the fractional part, so 1.9 becomes 1 and -1.9 becomes -1.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1.9, -1.9]).astype(int))

topics.title: Text becomes a number with astype
topics.body: Numeric strings cast cleanly to int or float, which is exactly why one bad token in a loaded column raises instead of silently becoming zero.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array(["1", "2"]).astype(float))

topics.title: Division always yields floats
topics.body: True division produces float64 even when both operands are integers, so `int / int` never silently loses the remainder.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print((np.array([1, 2]) / 2).dtype)

topics.title: Numbers become booleans by truthiness
topics.body: Casting to bool keeps only whether a value is non-zero, so 0 becomes False and every other number becomes True.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([0, 1, 2]).astype(bool))

topics.title: Count with a boolean array
topics.body: Booleans add as 1 and 0, so sum() on a mask counts the matches without any branching code.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.array([True, False, True])
print(m.sum())

topics.title: dtype reports the element type
topics.body: The dtype belongs to the whole array, not to each element. Mixing an int and a float array promotes to float.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([1, 2]).dtype, np.array([1.0]).dtype)

topics.title: A float array prints a decimal point
topics.body: The printed form already tells you the dtype: `[1. 2.]` is float, `[1 2]` is int. Reading the output is faster than checking.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([1, 2], dtype=float))

topics.title: Each dtype has a size in bytes
topics.body: `itemsize` is bytes per element. Ten million `int64` values need 80 MB before any copy, which is why dtype choice is a memory decision.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.dtype('int64').itemsize, np.dtype('int32').itemsize)

topics.title: A comparison produces booleans
topics.body: Masks are a dtype, not a special object. `bool` arrays are one byte per element and are the currency of filtering.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.array([1, 2, 3]) > 1).dtype)

modules.title: Array Indexing and Selection
modules.goal: Select single values, rows and columns with basic, negative and fancy indexing, and read IndexError correctly.

topics.title: Positive and negative indexing
topics.body: Index 0 is the first element and -1 is the last, so negative indices count from the end without needing the length.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(a[0], a[-1])

topics.title: Rows and cells in 2-D
topics.body: The first index selects the row and the second the column; one index alone returns that whole row as a 1-D array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a[1, 2], a[0])

topics.title: Fancy indexing with an index array
topics.body: Passing a list of positions returns a new array of those elements in the order you asked for, which is how you reorder or sample rows.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(a[[0, 2]])

topics.title: Index with a coordinate pair
topics.body: Two indices in one bracket address a single cell, row first then column, and the result is a scalar rather than an array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[1, 2])

topics.title: One index drops a dimension
topics.body: Indexing a single row of a (2, 3) array returns shape (3,), because that axis is consumed by the integer index.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[0].shape)

topics.title: Select a whole column
topics.body: A colon keeps the row axis and the integer picks the column, so `a[:, 1]` is the second column of every row.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[:, 1])

topics.title: Fancy indexing picks rows
topics.body: An array of indices selects in exactly the order you give it, so repeats and reordering are allowed and the output grows to match the index list.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[[0, 1, 0]])

topics.title: take works along an axis
topics.body: np.take does the same selection as fancy indexing but names the axis, which makes the intent readable in longer pipelines.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(np.take(a, [2, 0], axis=1))

topics.title: Negative indices count from the end
topics.body: `-1` is the last element, `-2` the one before it. The same rule applies to slices and to every axis.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a[-1], a[-2])

topics.title: Slice columns of a matrix
topics.body: The colon means "every row", the number picks one column. The result loses that axis and becomes one-dimensional.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[:, 1])

topics.title: A boolean mask filters one dimension
topics.body: The mask must match the array's shape. Elements where the mask is `True` are copied into a new, shorter array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([5, 6, 7])
print(a[a > 5])

topics.title: Index with paired row and column lists
topics.body: Two index arrays are zipped, not crossed: element `i` of the result comes from row `rows[i]`, column `cols[i]`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[[0, 2], [1, 2]])

debug.title: Off-by-one on a 1-D array
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a[3])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a[2])
debug.error: IndexError: index 3 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 3

debug.title: Column index outside the row
debug.broken:

a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a[0, 2])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a[0, 1])

debug.title: An index that is not an integer
debug.broken:

a = np.arange(4)
print(a[1.5])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[1])

modules.title: Slicing and Array Views
modules.goal: Slice arrays with start/stop/step, slice rows and columns, and know when a slice shares memory.

topics.title: Slice with a step
topics.body: A slice is start:stop:step and the stop is excluded; a step of 2 skips every other element, which is the fast way to downsample a series.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print(a[2:8:2])

topics.title: Slice rows and columns
topics.body: In 2-D the first slice selects rows and the second columns; `1:` keeps every column from index 1 onward.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[:2, 1:])

topics.title: A slice is a view
topics.body: Basic slicing returns a view, so writing into the slice writes into the original array — the most common source of "my data changed by itself".
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
b = a[1:3]
b[0] = 99
print(a)

topics.title: Reverse a row with a negative step
topics.body: A step of -1 walks the array backwards, so `a[::-1]` is the reversed view and needs no loop or copy.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[::-1])

topics.title: Slice assignment writes through
topics.body: Assigning into a slice edits the original array, because the slice is a window onto the same memory rather than a new array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
a[0:2] = 0
print(a)

topics.title: Step in both dimensions
topics.body: Each axis takes its own step, so `a[::2, ::2]` keeps every second row and every second column of a 2-D array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(16).reshape(4, 4)
print(a[::2, ::2])

topics.title: Copy breaks the view link
topics.body: Calling copy() allocates new memory, so changing the copy leaves the original untouched and the sharing problem disappears.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
b = a[:].copy()
b[0] = 9
print(a, b)

topics.title: Slices clamp instead of failing
topics.body: A slice bound past the end is clamped to the array length, so `a[0:100]` on three elements returns all three instead of raising.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
print(a[0:100])

topics.title: The end of a slice is exclusive
topics.body: `a[2:5]` keeps positions 2, 3 and 4. Off-by-one bugs in NumPy almost always come from forgetting this.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(10)
print(a[2:5])

topics.title: Omit a bound to keep it open
topics.body: `a[:2]` starts at zero, `a[3:]` runs to the end. Leaving a bound out is the idiomatic way to say "from the edge".
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(5)
print(a[:2], a[3:])

topics.title: A step of two skips elements
topics.body: The third slot of a slice is the step. It can be larger than one or negative, and it never changes the source array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.arange(10)[::2])

topics.title: Slice rows and columns at once
topics.body: Each axis gets its own slice separated by a comma. The result is a rectangular block, never a ragged one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[1:, :2])

learn.title: Slice with a step
learn.body: A slice is start:stop:step and the stop is excluded; a step of 2 skips every other element, which is the fast way to downsample a series.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print(a[2:8:2])

learn.title: Slice rows and columns
learn.body: In 2-D the first slice selects rows and the second columns; `1:` keeps every column from index 1 onward.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[:2, 1:])

learn.title: A slice is a view
learn.body: Basic slicing returns a view, so writing into the slice writes into the original array — the most common source of "my data changed by itself".
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
b = a[1:3]
b[0] = 99
print(a)

learn.title: Reverse a row with a negative step
learn.body: A step of -1 walks the array backwards, so `a[::-1]` is the reversed view and needs no loop or copy.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[::-1])

learn.title: Slice assignment writes through
learn.body: Assigning into a slice edits the original array, because the slice is a window onto the same memory rather than a new array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
a[0:2] = 0
print(a)

learn.title: Step in both dimensions
learn.body: Each axis takes its own step, so `a[::2, ::2]` keeps every second row and every second column of a 2-D array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(16).reshape(4, 4)
print(a[::2, ::2])

learn.title: Copy breaks the view link
learn.body: Calling copy() allocates new memory, so changing the copy leaves the original untouched and the sharing problem disappears.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
b = a[:].copy()
b[0] = 9
print(a, b)

learn.title: Slices clamp instead of failing
learn.body: A slice bound past the end is clamped to the array length, so `a[0:100]` on three elements returns all three instead of raising.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
print(a[0:100])

learn.title: The end of a slice is exclusive
learn.body: `a[2:5]` keeps positions 2, 3 and 4. Off-by-one bugs in NumPy almost always come from forgetting this.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(10)
print(a[2:5])

learn.title: Omit a bound to keep it open
learn.body: `a[:2]` starts at zero, `a[3:]` runs to the end. Leaving a bound out is the idiomatic way to say "from the edge".
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(5)
print(a[:2], a[3:])

learn.title: A step of two skips elements
learn.body: The third slot of a slice is the step. It can be larger than one or negative, and it never changes the source array.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.arange(10)[::2])

learn.title: Slice rows and columns at once
learn.body: Each axis gets its own slice separated by a comma. The result is a rectangular block, never a ragged one.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[1:, :2])

print(a[::-1])

checkpoint.q: In your own words: what does reverse a row with a negative step do?
checkpoint.answer: A step of -1 walks the array backwards, so `a[::-1]` is the reversed view and needs no loop or copy.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint: predict the output of this code about slice assignment writes through.
checkpoint.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
a[0:2] = 0
print(a)

checkpoint.q: In your own words: what does slice assignment writes through do?
checkpoint.answer: Assigning into a slice edits the original array, because the slice is a window onto the same memory rather than a new array.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint: predict the output of this code about step in both dimensions.
checkpoint.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(16).reshape(4, 4)
print(a[::2, ::2])

checkpoint.q: In your own words: what does step in both dimensions do?
checkpoint.answer: Each axis takes its own step, so `a[::2, ::2]` keeps every second row and every second column of a 2-D array.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint: predict the output of this code about copy breaks the view link.
checkpoint.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
b = a[:].copy()
b[0] = 9
print(a, b)

checkpoint.q: In your own words: what does copy breaks the view link do?
checkpoint.answer: Calling copy() allocates new memory, so changing the copy leaves the original untouched and the sharing problem disappears.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint: predict the output of this code about slices clamp instead of failing.
checkpoint.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
print(a[0:100])

checkpoint.q: In your own words: what does slices clamp instead of failing do?
checkpoint.answer: A slice bound past the end is clamped to the array length, so `a[0:100]` on three elements returns all three instead of raising.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint: predict the output of this code about the end of a slice is exclusive.
checkpoint.code:

a = np.arange(10)
print(a[2:5])

checkpoint.q: In your own words: what does the end of a slice is exclusive do?
checkpoint.answer: `a[2:5]` keeps positions 2, 3 and 4. Off-by-one bugs in NumPy almost always come from forgetting this.

checkpoint.q: Checkpoint: predict the output of this code about omit a bound to keep it open.

a = np.arange(5)
print(a[:2], a[3:])

checkpoint.q: In your own words: what does omit a bound to keep it open do?
checkpoint.answer: `a[:2]` starts at zero, `a[3:]` runs to the end. Leaving a bound out is the idiomatic way to say "from the edge".

checkpoint.q: In your own words: what does a step of two skips elements do?

modules.title: Array Reshaping and Manipulation
modules.goal: Reshape, flatten, transpose, combine and split arrays so data fits the shape an operation needs.

topics.title: reshape
topics.body: reshape changes the shape without changing the data or its order; the element count must stay the same, so 6 values can become (2, 3) but never (4, 2).
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a)

topics.title: ravel and transpose
topics.body: ravel flattens to one dimension (often as a view) and .T swaps rows with columns; together they move a matrix between the two layouts most libraries expect.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.ravel(), a.T)

topics.title: concatenate and stack
topics.body: concatenate joins along an existing axis and stack creates a NEW axis, which is why two length-2 arrays stack into a (2, 2) matrix.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2])
print(np.concatenate([a, a]), np.stack([a, a]).shape)

topics.title: reshape with -1 infers the size
topics.body: One dimension may be written as -1 and NumPy fills it from the element count, which is how you ask for rows of a fixed width without arithmetic.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a.reshape(-1, 2))

topics.title: newaxis makes a column
topics.body: Indexing with np.newaxis inserts an axis of length 1, turning a (3,) vector into a (3, 1) column that broadcasting can line up against rows.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(3)[:, np.newaxis].shape)

topics.title: stack adds a new axis
topics.body: stack joins arrays of equal shape along a brand-new axis, so two (2,) arrays become a (2, 2) matrix instead of a (4,) flat one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.stack([np.zeros(2), np.ones(2)]).shape)

topics.title: split cuts an array into pieces
topics.body: split divides an array into equal parts and returns a list, which is handy for batches or train/test cuts.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.split(np.arange(4), 2))

topics.title: flatten always copies
topics.body: flatten returns a fresh 1-D array, so editing it never touches the source; ravel returns a view whenever the layout allows.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
f = a.flatten()
f[0] = 9
print(a[0])

topics.title: ravel flattens without copying when it can
topics.body: A contiguous array can be flattened as a view. `base` proves whether the new array still points at the old memory.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.ravel().base is a)

topics.title: reshape turns a vector into a column
topics.body: `(4, 1)` and `(1, 4)` look similar but broadcast in opposite directions. The shape is the whole difference.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(4)
print(a.reshape(4, 1))

topics.title: vstack stacks arrays into rows
topics.body: `vstack` adds a new first axis, so two `(2,)` arrays become one `(2, 2)` array. `hstack` joins along the existing axis instead.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.vstack([np.array([1, 2]), np.array([3, 4])]))

topics.title: Transpose swaps the axes
topics.body: `.T` reverses the axis order and is a view, not a copy. For a matrix it swaps rows with columns.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.T.shape)

modules.title: Array Operations and Universal Functions
modules.goal: Use arithmetic, math and comparison ufuncs elementwise, and read a ufunc type error correctly.

topics.title: Arithmetic is elementwise
topics.body: Operators on arrays are universal functions applied element by element; `a + 1` adds to every element and `a ** 2` squares each one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a + 1, a ** 2)

topics.title: Math ufuncs
topics.body: sqrt, exp and log are the same elementwise functions for arrays and scalars, so one call replaces a comprehension.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sqrt(9), np.exp(0), np.log(1))

topics.title: Comparisons produce masks
topics.body: A comparison returns a boolean array of the same shape, and indexing the array with that mask keeps only the True positions.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 5, 3])
print(a > 2, a[a > 2])

topics.title: sqrt of perfect squares is exact
topics.body: Universal functions run compiled loops over the whole array, so np.sqrt returns a float array of the same shape in one call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sqrt([4, 9, 25]))

topics.title: reduce sums, accumulate keeps running totals
topics.body: Every binary ufunc offers reduce (fold the whole array to one value) and accumulate (return every intermediate total).
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.add.reduce([1, 2, 3]), np.add.accumulate([1, 2, 3]))

topics.title: clip limits every element
topics.body: clip pins values into a range without a single if, which is how pixel and probability pipelines stay inside their legal bounds.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.clip([0, 5, 10], 1, 8))

topics.title: round, floor and ceil differ
topics.body: round goes to the nearest even integer at .5, floor always drops down and ceil always climbs, so pick the one your data means.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.round([1.5, 2.4]), np.floor([1.5, 2.4]), np.ceil([1.5, 2.4]))

topics.title: sign tells you direction
topics.body: np.sign maps negatives to -1, zero to 0 and positives to 1, giving a direction array you can multiply into other data.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sign([-3, 0, 5]))

topics.title: Exponentiation uses the ** operator
topics.body: `**` is elementwise on arrays. `np.power` is the same operation written as a function when you need it as a callback.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([2, 3]) ** 2)

topics.title: abs works on whole arrays
topics.body: NumPy's functions accept arrays, lists and scalars through the same call. That consistency is what makes them composable.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.abs(np.array([-3, 4])))

topics.title: cumsum keeps every running total
topics.body: `cumsum` returns an array of the same length, while `sum` collapses it to one number. Use the cumulative form for running balances and charts.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.cumsum(np.array([1, 2, 3])))

topics.title: log and exp invert each other
topics.body: Applying `exp` after `log` returns the original numbers up to floating-point error, which is exactly what `allclose` is for.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

values = np.array([1.0, 10.0])
print(np.allclose(np.exp(np.log(values)), values))

interview.q: What does this cumsum keeps every running total snippet print, and why?
interview.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.cumsum(np.array([1, 2, 3])))

interview.q: What is log and exp invert each other, and when would you use it?
interview.answer: Applying `exp` after `log` returns the original numbers up to floating-point error, which is exactly what `allclose` is for.

interview.q: What does this log and exp invert each other snippet print, and why?
interview.code:
import numpy as np

values = np.array([1.0, 10.0])
print(np.allclose(np.exp(np.log(values)), values))
interview.answer: True

modules.title: Broadcasting
modules.goal: Apply the broadcasting rules to scalars, rows and columns, and fix incompatible-shape errors.

topics.title: Scalar broadcasting
topics.body: A scalar is stretched across every element without being copied, which is why `a + 10` is both simple and memory-cheap.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a + 10)

topics.title: Row and column broadcasting
topics.body: Shapes are compared from the right: (2, 3) with (3,) lines up the 3s, so each column is scaled by its own weight.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
w = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a * w)

topics.title: Incompatible shapes fail loudly
topics.body: If two sizes disagree and neither is 1, NumPy raises ValueError instead of guessing; that error is the rule working, not a bug.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
b = np.ones((2, 2))
try:
    a + b
except ValueError:
    print('broadcast error')

topics.title: A vector broadcasts across rows
topics.body: A (3,) vector added to a (2, 3) matrix is treated as one row repeated per matrix row, so the column count has to match.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3), dtype=int)
print(a + np.array([1, 2, 3]))

topics.title: A column broadcasts down
topics.body: A (2, 1) column is stretched across every column, which is how one value per row is applied to a whole matrix.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3), dtype=int)
print(a + np.array([[10], [20]]))

topics.title: Outer product uses two new axes
topics.body: Adding an axis to each operand makes broadcasting compute every pair, which is the outer product without writing a loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2])
b = np.array([3, 4])
print(a[:, None] * b[None, :])

topics.title: Comparison broadcasts too
topics.body: Broadcasting is not limited to arithmetic: comparing a matrix with its per-column mean stretches the mean across rows.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[3, 1, 2], [6, 5, 4]])
print(a > a.mean(axis=0))

topics.title: reshape prepares a strip for broadcasting
topics.body: Turning a vector into a (3, 1) column and adding a (1, 2) row yields a (3, 2) grid, which is the shape rule worth memorising.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
v = np.arange(3)
print((v.reshape(3, 1) + np.zeros((1, 2))).shape)

topics.title: A row array broadcasts across rows
topics.body: A `(3,)` array lines up with the last axis of a `(2, 3)` array. That is the rule that makes row-wise maths a single line.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.ones((2, 3))
print((a + np.array([1, 2, 3])).shape)

topics.title: A scalar is the smallest broadcast
topics.body: Scalars stretch to every position without copying. The result is a new array of the original shape.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.ones((2, 2)) * 3).tolist())

topics.title: Broadcast a column against a row
topics.body: A `(2, 1)` column and a `(2,)` row produce a `(2, 2)` grid — every combination, with no explicit loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.array([[1], [2]]) * np.array([10, 20])).tolist())

topics.title: A size of one stretches automatically
topics.body: An axis of length 1 is repeated to match the other operand. That is why `(3, 1) + ones(4)` becomes `(3, 4)`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.zeros((3, 1)) + np.ones(4)).shape)

debug.title: A (2,) vector against (2, 3)
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2,))
b = np.ones((2, 3))
print(a + b)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 1))
b = np.ones((2, 3))
print(a + b)
debug.error: ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (2,) (2,3)

debug.title: Transposed shape by mistake
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 3))
b = np.zeros((3, 2))
print(a * b)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 3))
b = np.zeros((3, 2))
print(a * b.T)
debug.error: ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (2,3) (3,2)

debug.title: A row vector where a column was needed
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
v = np.array([1, 2])
print(a + v)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
v = np.array([1, 2]).reshape(2, 1)
print(a + v)

lab.brief: Apply three per-feature weights to a (4, 3) batch and prove the output shape stays (4, 3).

tasks.title: Add per-row offsets
tasks.statement: Add `np.array([10, 20])` to every row of `np.ones((3, 2))` and store the result.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = np.ones((3, 2)) + np.array([10, 20])
print(result)

tasks.title: Multiply a column by a row
tasks.statement: Multiply `np.array([[1], [2], [3]])` by `np.array([1, 10, 100])` and store the 3x3 result in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = np.array([[1], [2], [3]]) * np.array([1, 10, 100])
print(result)

tasks.title: Shape of a broadcast sum
tasks.statement: Store the shape of `np.zeros((4, 1)) + np.ones(3)` in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
result = (np.zeros((4, 1)) + np.ones(3)).shape
print(result)

tasks.title: Centre each column on its mean
tasks.statement: Subtract each column's mean from `np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 6.0]])` and store the centred array in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 6.0]])
result = a - a.mean(axis=0)
print(result)

learn.title: Scalar broadcasting
learn.body: A scalar is stretched across every element without being copied, which is why `a + 10` is both simple and memory-cheap.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a + 10)

learn.title: Row and column broadcasting
learn.body: Shapes are compared from the right: (2, 3) with (3,) lines up the 3s, so each column is scaled by its own weight.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
w = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a * w)

learn.title: Incompatible shapes fail loudly
learn.body: If two sizes disagree and neither is 1, NumPy raises ValueError instead of guessing; that error is the rule working, not a bug.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
b = np.ones((2, 2))
try:
    a + b
except ValueError:
    print('broadcast error')

learn.title: A vector broadcasts across rows
learn.body: A (3,) vector added to a (2, 3) matrix is treated as one row repeated per matrix row, so the column count has to match.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3), dtype=int)
print(a + np.array([1, 2, 3]))

learn.title: A column broadcasts down
learn.body: A (2, 1) column is stretched across every column, which is how one value per row is applied to a whole matrix.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3), dtype=int)
print(a + np.array([[10], [20]]))

learn.title: Outer product uses two new axes
learn.body: Adding an axis to each operand makes broadcasting compute every pair, which is the outer product without writing a loop.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2])
b = np.array([3, 4])
print(a[:, None] * b[None, :])

learn.title: Comparison broadcasts too
learn.body: Broadcasting is not limited to arithmetic: comparing a matrix with its per-column mean stretches the mean across rows.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[3, 1, 2], [6, 5, 4]])
print(a > a.mean(axis=0))

learn.title: reshape prepares a strip for broadcasting
learn.body: Turning a vector into a (3, 1) column and adding a (1, 2) row yields a (3, 2) grid, which is the shape rule worth memorising.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
v = np.arange(3)
print((v.reshape(3, 1) + np.zeros((1, 2))).shape)

learn.title: A row array broadcasts across rows
learn.body: A `(3,)` array lines up with the last axis of a `(2, 3)` array. That is the rule that makes row-wise maths a single line.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.ones((2, 3))
print((a + np.array([1, 2, 3])).shape)

learn.title: A scalar is the smallest broadcast
learn.body: Scalars stretch to every position without copying. The result is a new array of the original shape.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.ones((2, 2)) * 3).tolist())

learn.title: Broadcast a column against a row
learn.body: A `(2, 1)` column and a `(2,)` row produce a `(2, 2)` grid — every combination, with no explicit loop.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.array([[1], [2]]) * np.array([10, 20])).tolist())

learn.title: A size of one stretches automatically
learn.body: An axis of length 1 is repeated to match the other operand. That is why `(3, 1) + ones(4)` becomes `(3, 4)`.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print((np.zeros((3, 1)) + np.ones(4)).shape)

modules.title: Aggregation and Statistics
modules.goal: Summarise arrays with sum, mean, std, argmin and cumulative functions along a chosen axis.

topics.title: Mean along an axis
topics.body: Without an axis every element is reduced to one number; with axis=1 each ROW is reduced, so a (2, 2) array gives two means.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.mean(), a.mean(axis=1))

topics.title: Standard deviation and variance
topics.body: var is the mean squared deviation and std is its square root; both use ddof=0 by default, which is the population form.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(a.std(), a.var())

topics.title: Position and running totals
topics.body: argmin returns WHERE the smallest value is (not the value) and cumsum returns the running total at every position.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([3, 1, 2])
print(a.argmin(), a.cumsum())

topics.title: median is not the mean
topics.body: One extreme value drags the mean but barely moves the median, so reporting both is how you notice a skewed column.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.median([1, 2, 100]), np.mean([1, 2, 100]))

topics.title: keepdims keeps a column
topics.body: keepdims=True leaves the reduced axis as length 1, so the result still broadcasts against the original array without a reshape.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True).shape)

topics.title: average can weight values
topics.body: np.average accepts weights, so a weighted mean is one call instead of a manual sum of products divided by a sum of weights.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.average([1, 2], weights=[1, 3]))

topics.title: any and all answer yes/no
topics.body: On a boolean array, any asks whether at least one element is True and all asks whether every element is, each returning a single bool.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.array([True, False])
print(m.any(), m.all())

topics.title: prod multiplies the elements
topics.body: prod folds with multiplication instead of addition, which is how compound growth and factorial-style products are computed in one call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.prod(np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])))

topics.title: mean of a matrix returns one number
topics.body: Without `axis`, a reduction flattens the array first. The result is a scalar, not a one-element array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]).mean())

topics.title: axis=1 reduces each row
topics.body: The reduced axis disappears. Row sums are therefore one value per row, in a `(2,)` array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]).sum(axis=1).tolist())

topics.title: std measures spread in the same units
topics.body: Variance is squared units; the standard deviation puts it back in the original scale, which is why reports use it.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.array([2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9]).std())

topics.title: The maximum and where it lives
topics.body: `max` gives the value, `argmax` gives its position. Both accept an `axis` when you need one answer per row.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([3, 9, 4])
print(a.max(), a.argmax())

modules.title: Boolean Indexing and Filtering
modules.goal: Filter arrays with masks, replace values with where and test membership with isin.

topics.title: Filter with a mask
topics.body: A comparison builds a boolean array; indexing with it keeps the True positions and returns a new array of the passing values.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([55, 72, 38])
print(a[a >= 60])

topics.title: np.where chooses without a loop
topics.body: where(condition, x, y) returns x where the condition is True and y where it is False, so a label column is one call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 5, 3])
print(np.where(a > 2, 'big', 'small'))

topics.title: Membership with isin
topics.body: isin answers "is each element in this list?" and returns a mask, which composes with other masks for multi-condition filters.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(np.isin(a, [2, 4]))

topics.title: Combine masks with & and |
topics.body: Elementwise combination needs the bitwise operators inside parentheses; `and` and `or` would ask for one truth value and fail.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a[(a > 1) & (a < 4)])

topics.title: Invert a mask with ~
topics.body: The tilde flips a boolean array, so `a[~(a > 1)]` keeps exactly the elements the mask rejected.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a[~(a > 1)])

topics.title: Assign through a mask
topics.body: A boolean mask works on the left of an assignment, which replaces the selected elements in place instead of returning a new array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([-1, 4, -5])
a[a < 0] = 0
print(a)

topics.title: Count how many match
topics.body: Because True is 1, summing a mask gives the count directly — no filter and no len call needed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print((a % 2 == 0).sum())

topics.title: Filter rows by one column
topics.body: A mask built from one column can select whole rows, so `a[a[:, 1] > 5]` keeps every column of the rows that qualify.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 9], [2, 3]])
print(a[a[:, 1] > 5])

topics.title: A mask keeps the shape of its array
topics.body: Comparing an array to a number never shortens it. Only indexing with the mask does that.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(5)
print((a % 2 == 0).shape)

topics.title: where chooses between two values
topics.body: `np.where(mask, a, b)` is a vectorised `if`. Neither branch is skipped, so both should be cheap expressions.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.where(np.array([1, 5, 2]) > 3, 'big', 'small').tolist())

topics.title: Sum the mask to count matches
topics.body: `True` counts as 1 and `False` as 0, so `sum` on a mask is a count. Wrap it in `int` when you want a Python number.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(int((np.arange(10) > 5).sum()))

topics.title: Filter a matrix elementwise
topics.body: Indexing with a full-shape mask flattens the matches into a 1-D array. Row structure is not preserved.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[a % 2 == 0].tolist())

debug.title: A mask shorter than the array
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a[[True, False]])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a[[True, False, True]])

modules.title: Sorting, Searching and Set Operations
modules.goal: Sort along an axis, recover order with argsort, locate insertion points and compare sets of values.

topics.title: sort and argsort
topics.body: np.sort returns a sorted copy while argsort returns the INDICES that would sort the array — the second is what you use to reorder parallel arrays.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([3, 1, 2])
print(np.sort(a), np.argsort(a))

topics.title: searchsorted
topics.body: searchsorted finds the insertion index that keeps a sorted array ordered, which is how you bucket a value without scanning.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 3, 5])
print(np.searchsorted(a, 4))

topics.title: Unique values and set operations
topics.body: unique returns sorted distinct values and intersect1d/union1d/setdiff1d answer the set questions directly on arrays.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 2, 3])
print(np.unique(a), np.intersect1d(a, [2, 4]))

topics.title: sort each row separately
topics.body: axis=1 sorts inside each row and leaves rows in place, while axis=0 would sort down each column instead.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[3, 1, 2], [9, 7, 8]])
print(np.sort(a, axis=1))

topics.title: Reverse a sorted array for descending order
topics.body: sort only goes ascending, so descending order is a sort followed by a reverse slice — two views, no extra list.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sort([3, 1, 2])[::-1])

modules.title: Copies, Views, Strides and Memory
modules.goal: Tell a view from a copy, prove sharing with shares_memory, and read strides and contiguity.

topics.title: view shares, copy does not
topics.body: a.view() shares the same buffer so a write through the view changes the original; a.copy() allocates new memory and leaves the original alone.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
v = a.view()
c = a.copy()
v[0] = 9
print(a, c)

topics.title: Prove sharing with shares_memory
topics.body: Slicing usually returns a view, but an explicit copy never shares; shares_memory answers the question with a real check instead of a guess.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(np.shares_memory(a, a[1:3]), np.shares_memory(a, a.copy()))

topics.title: Strides describe memory steps
topics.body: strides are the bytes to move per axis; a (2, 3) int64 array steps 24 bytes per row and 8 bytes per column, which is why layout affects speed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.strides)

topics.title: reshape usually returns a view
topics.body: When the memory is contiguous, reshape hands back a new shape over the same buffer, so shares_memory is True and writes travel both ways.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
b = a.reshape(2, 3)
print(np.shares_memory(a, b))

topics.title: base points at the source array
topics.body: A view keeps a reference to the array it came from in .base, which is the quickest way to prove two names share one buffer.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
print(a[1:].base is a)

topics.title: Transpose is a view with new strides
topics.body: Transposing changes only the strides, not the data, so a (2, 3) float64 array transposes to strides (8, 24) with the same bytes.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a.T.strides)

topics.title: A reversed slice has negative strides
topics.body: A step of -1 stores a negative stride, which is why reversing is free: the array simply walks its memory backwards.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(4)[::-1].strides)

topics.title: copy owns its memory
topics.body: The OWNDATA flag tells you whether an array owns its buffer or borrows it, which is the truth behind the view/copy question.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
print(a.copy().flags['OWNDATA'])

topics.title: A slice is a view into the source
topics.body: Assigning into the slice writes into the original buffer. Nothing was copied when the slice was taken.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(4)
b = a[:2]
b[0] = 99
print(a.tolist())

topics.title: A copy stops the sharing
topics.body: `.copy()` allocates a new buffer, so writes to it never reach the source. This is the fix for accidental mutation.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(4)
b = a[:2].copy()
b[0] = 99
print(a.tolist())

topics.title: Strides describe how memory is walked
topics.body: The stride is bytes to step per axis. A transposed or sliced array needs no new memory because only the strides change.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3).strides)

topics.title: A reshape can stay a view
topics.body: If the layout allows it, `reshape` returns a view whose `base` is the original array. A transpose or a non-contiguous slice forces a copy.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.arange(6)
b = a.reshape(2, 3)
print(b.base is a)

debug.title: Adding to a view rebound the name
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
b = a.view()
b = b + 1
print(a)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(4)
b = a.view()
b += 1
print(a)
debug.error: prints [0 1 2 3] — b + 1 created a new array, so the view was lost

debug.title: Strides are read-only
debug.broken:

a = np.arange(4)
a.strides = (1,)
debug.fix:

a = np.arange(4)
print(a.strides)

debug.fix:

a = np.arange(3)
print(a.flags['OWNDATA'])

modules.title: Random Number Generation
modules.goal: Use default_rng, reproduce runs with a seed, and sample from the common distributions.

topics.title: default_rng and reproducibility
topics.body: default_rng(seed) returns a Generator; the same seed reproduces the same stream on every run, which is what makes a simulation debuggable.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
a = rng.integers(0, 10, 3)
print(len(a), a.min() >= 0, a.max() < 10)

topics.title: Normal draws
topics.body: rng.normal(loc, scale, size) samples a Gaussian; rounding the printed values keeps a demo readable without changing the data.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
print(rng.normal(0, 1, 2).shape)

topics.title: choice and shuffle
topics.body: choice samples with replacement by default (replace=False for a draw without repeats) and shuffle reorders an array in place.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
print(len(np.unique(rng.choice([1, 2, 3], 2, replace=False))))

topics.title: integers draw inside a half-open range
topics.body: integers(low, high) returns values from low up to but excluding high, and the seeded generator makes the draw reproducible.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
print(rng.integers(1, 7, 5))

topics.title: random floats sit between 0 and 1
topics.body: random returns floats in [0, 1), which you scale and shift into any interval you need.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
print(rng.random(3).round(3))

topics.title: the same seed gives the same numbers
topics.body: Two generators built with the same seed produce identical streams, which is the whole reason experiments are reproducible.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.random.default_rng(7).normal(size=2)
b = np.random.default_rng(7).normal(size=2)
print(np.allclose(a, b))

topics.title: size controls the shape of a draw
topics.body: Passing a tuple to size returns a multi-dimensional draw, so a batch of samples is one call instead of a loop of calls.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
print(rng.normal(size=(2, 3)).shape)

topics.title: permutation shuffles a copy
topics.body: permutation returns a shuffled copy and leaves the input alone, so sorting the result recovers the original values exactly.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
print(np.sort(rng.permutation(5)))

topics.title: integers excludes the high value
topics.body: `rng.integers(low, high)` is half-open, like `range`. Asking for `(0, 2)` can only yield 0 or 1.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
print(rng.integers(0, 2, size=5).max() <= 1)

topics.title: The seed decides the whole stream
topics.body: Two generators made with the same seed produce identical draws. That is how a random example becomes reproducible.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

first = np.random.default_rng(42).random(3).round(3).tolist()
second = np.random.default_rng(42).random(3).round(3).tolist()
print(first == second)

topics.title: choice samples without replacement
topics.body: `replace=False` behaves like drawing cards: no value repeats. With `replace=True` a value can appear several times.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
draw = rng.choice(5, 3, replace=False)
print(len(set(draw.tolist())) == 3)

topics.title: normal draws cluster around the mean
topics.body: The mean of many standard normal draws approaches zero. Increasing the sample size tightens the estimate, not the spread.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
sample = rng.normal(0, 1, 10000)
print(abs(sample.mean()) < 0.05)

tasks.title: A shuffle keeps the values
tasks.statement: Shuffle `np.arange(5)` with a seeded generator and store `True` in `result` if the shuffled values are still 0 to 4 in some order, otherwise `False`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
shuffled = rng.permutation(np.arange(5))
result = sorted(shuffled.tolist()) == [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
print(result)

tasks.title: Four distinct picks
tasks.statement: Draw 4 values from 0 to 5 without replacement using `np.random.default_rng(3)` and store how many distinct values you got, as an int, in `result`.
tasks.solution:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
draw = rng.choice(6, 4, replace=False)
result = int(len(set(draw.tolist())))
print(result)
tasks.check: assert result == 4, f'expected 4 distinct picks, got {result!r}'

learn.title: default_rng and reproducibility
learn.body: default_rng(seed) returns a Generator; the same seed reproduces the same stream on every run, which is what makes a simulation debuggable.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
a = rng.integers(0, 10, 3)
print(len(a), a.min() >= 0, a.max() < 10)

learn.title: Normal draws
learn.body: rng.normal(loc, scale, size) samples a Gaussian; rounding the printed values keeps a demo readable without changing the data.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
print(rng.normal(0, 1, 2).shape)

learn.title: choice and shuffle
learn.body: choice samples with replacement by default (replace=False for a draw without repeats) and shuffle reorders an array in place.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
print(len(np.unique(rng.choice([1, 2, 3], 2, replace=False))))

learn.title: integers draw inside a half-open range
learn.body: integers(low, high) returns values from low up to but excluding high, and the seeded generator makes the draw reproducible.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
print(rng.integers(1, 7, 5))

learn.title: random floats sit between 0 and 1
learn.body: random returns floats in [0, 1), which you scale and shift into any interval you need.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
print(rng.random(3).round(3))

learn.title: the same seed gives the same numbers
learn.body: Two generators built with the same seed produce identical streams, which is the whole reason experiments are reproducible.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.random.default_rng(7).normal(size=2)
b = np.random.default_rng(7).normal(size=2)
print(np.allclose(a, b))

learn.title: size controls the shape of a draw
learn.body: Passing a tuple to size returns a multi-dimensional draw, so a batch of samples is one call instead of a loop of calls.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
print(rng.normal(size=(2, 3)).shape)

learn.title: permutation shuffles a copy
learn.body: permutation returns a shuffled copy and leaves the input alone, so sorting the result recovers the original values exactly.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
print(np.sort(rng.permutation(5)))

learn.title: integers excludes the high value
learn.body: `rng.integers(low, high)` is half-open, like `range`. Asking for `(0, 2)` can only yield 0 or 1.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
print(rng.integers(0, 2, size=5).max() <= 1)

learn.title: The seed decides the whole stream
learn.body: Two generators made with the same seed produce identical draws. That is how a random example becomes reproducible.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

first = np.random.default_rng(42).random(3).round(3).tolist()
second = np.random.default_rng(42).random(3).round(3).tolist()
print(first == second)

learn.title: choice samples without replacement
learn.body: `replace=False` behaves like drawing cards: no value repeats. With `replace=True` a value can appear several times.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
draw = rng.choice(5, 3, replace=False)
print(len(set(draw.tolist())) == 3)

learn.title: normal draws cluster around the mean
learn.body: The mean of many standard normal draws approaches zero. Increasing the sample size tightens the estimate, not the spread.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
sample = rng.normal(0, 1, 10000)
print(abs(sample.mean()) < 0.05)

modules.title: Linear Algebra
modules.goal: Multiply matrices, solve systems with solve instead of inv, and read determinant and eigenvalue output.

topics.title: Matrix multiplication
topics.body: The @ operator (and np.matmul) performs matrix multiplication, not elementwise multiplication; multiplying by an identity returns the same matrix.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
B = np.eye(2)
print(A @ B)

topics.title: Solve instead of invert
topics.body: np.linalg.solve(A, b) solves Ax = b directly and is numerically safer and faster than computing inv(A) @ b.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 3.]])
b = np.array([5., 10.])
print(np.linalg.solve(A, b))

topics.title: Determinant and eigenvalues
topics.body: det tells you whether a matrix is singular and eigvals returns the eigenvalues; for a diagonal matrix those eigenvalues are the diagonal entries.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., 0.], [0., 3.]])
print(np.linalg.det(A), np.linalg.eigvals(A).real)

topics.title: dot product of two vectors is a scalar
topics.body: The @ operator on two 1-D arrays sums the pairwise products, so the result is a scalar rather than an array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([4, 5, 6])
print(a @ b)

topics.title: matrix times vector keeps the rows
topics.body: A (2, 2) matrix times a (2,) vector returns one value per row, so the output length is the number of rows.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
v = np.array([1, 1])
print(A @ v)

topics.title: solve then verify
topics.body: solve returns the x in Ax = b directly; checking A @ x against b is how you prove the answer instead of trusting it.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 3.]])
b = np.array([3., 5.])
x = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
print(x, np.allclose(A @ x, b))

topics.title: norm measures length
topics.body: np.linalg.norm gives the Euclidean length by default, so a (3, 4) vector reports 5.0 and needs no manual square root.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.linalg.norm([3, 4]))

topics.title: lstsq also fits inconsistent systems
topics.body: When the system has no exact solution, lstsq returns the least-squares answer so a tall, over-determined fit still works.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1., 0.], [0., 1.], [1., 1.]])
b = np.array([1., 2., 3.])
x = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)[0]
print(np.allclose(A @ x, b))

topics.title: identity is the matrix version of one
topics.body: Multiplying by `np.identity(n)` leaves a matrix unchanged. It is the natural sanity check for a matmul pipeline.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 3.0]])
print(np.allclose(A @ np.identity(2), A))

topics.title: Transpose flips a matrix product
topics.body: `(A @ B).T` equals `B.T @ A.T`. The order swaps, which is the property behind many derivations.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]])
B = np.array([[0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 0.0]])
print(np.allclose((A @ B).T, B.T @ A.T))

topics.title: A zero determinant means no unique solution
topics.body: A singular matrix has linearly dependent rows, so `solve` cannot return one answer. Check the determinant before trusting a fit.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(round(float(np.linalg.det(np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [2.0, 4.0]]))), 6))

topics.title: trace sums the diagonal
topics.body: The trace needs no square-matrix maths beyond the diagonal. It equals the sum of the eigenvalues.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.trace(np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])))

modules.title: NumPy File Input and Output
modules.goal: Persist arrays with save/load, read text and CSV data, and pack several arrays into one NPZ file.

topics.title: save and load
topics.body: np.save writes the array's bytes and dtype to a .npy file and np.load reads them back exactly; the file is binary, so text editors show noise.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
np.save('/tmp/a.npy', np.arange(3))
print(np.load('/tmp/a.npy'))

topics.title: Text and CSV round-trip
topics.body: savetxt writes human-readable numbers and loadtxt parses them back as floats, which is the portable option when another tool must read the file.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
np.savetxt('/tmp/a.txt', np.array([1, 2]))
print(np.loadtxt('/tmp/a.txt'))

topics.title: Several arrays in one NPZ
topics.body: savez stores named arrays in a single compressed-free archive and load returns a mapping whose keys are the names you gave.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
np.savez('/tmp/a.npz', x=np.arange(2))
print(list(np.load('/tmp/a.npz').keys()))

topics.title: skiprows ignores a header line
topics.body: loadtxt has no header concept, so skiprows=1 is how a CSV header is dropped before the numbers are parsed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np, os, tempfile
p = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'np_head.csv')
open(p, 'w').write('x,y\n1,2\n3,4\n')
print(np.loadtxt(p, delimiter=',', skiprows=1))

topics.title: genfromtxt fills missing values
topics.body: genfromtxt tolerates gaps and puts nan where a value is absent, which is exactly what loadtxt would refuse to parse.
topics.code:
import numpy as np, os, tempfile

modules.title: Advanced Data Types and Special Arrays
modules.goal: Use structured dtypes, datetime64 and vectorised string operations for real records.

topics.title: Structured arrays
topics.body: A structured dtype names each field and its type, so one array can hold an id and a score and you can select a column with a['field'].
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([(1, 2.5)], dtype=[('id', 'i4'), ('score', 'f4')])
print(a['score'])

topics.title: datetime64 arithmetic
topics.body: A datetime64 array with a unit such as [D] supports addition of whole days, so date maths stays integer arithmetic underneath.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
d = np.array(['2026-01-01'], dtype='datetime64[D]')
print(d + 1)

topics.title: Vectorised string operations
topics.body: np.char applies string methods elementwise; it is convenient for arrays of text but it is not a replacement for proper text tooling.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array(['num', 'py'])
print(np.char.upper(a))

topics.title: Fixed-width strings truncate
topics.body: A U2 dtype stores at most two characters per element, so longer text is cut on creation rather than at print time.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array(["abcd"], dtype="U2"))

topics.title: object dtype keeps Python objects
topics.body: dtype=object stores pointers to arbitrary Python values, which is flexible but loses the fast numeric paths that make arrays worthwhile.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, "x", None], dtype=object)
print(a.dtype, a[1])

topics.title: timedelta64 tells the gap
topics.body: Subtracting two datetime64 values returns a timedelta64, so date arithmetic reports an interval in the unit of the operands.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.datetime64('2024-01-03') - np.datetime64('2024-01-01'))

topics.title: Divide a timedelta to get a count
topics.body: Dividing a timedelta64 by a unit timedelta converts it to a plain number, which is how you get days, hours or seconds for analysis.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
d = np.datetime64('2024-01-03') - np.datetime64('2024-01-01')
print(d / np.timedelta64(1, 'D'))

topics.title: Fields are read by name
topics.body: A structured array indexes its fields by name, so a price column is a plain array you can sum without unpacking the records.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([(1, 2.5), (2, 3.5)], dtype=[('id', 'i4'), ('price', 'f4')])
print(a['price'].sum())

topics.title: char functions work elementwise on text
topics.body: The `np.char` namespace applies string methods to every element without a Python loop.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.char.upper(np.array(['np', 'ai'])).tolist())

topics.title: str_len counts characters
topics.body: Length is a property of the string, not the fixed-width buffer. Padding does not inflate the count.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.char.str_len(np.array(['ab', 'cde'])).tolist())

topics.title: Datetime differences are timedeltas
topics.body: Subtracting two `datetime64` values gives a `timedelta64`, which converts to a number by dividing by a unit.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

start = np.datetime64('2026-01-01')
end = np.datetime64('2026-01-11')
print((end - start) / np.timedelta64(1, 'D'))

topics.title: A structured array reads fields by name
topics.body: One row can hold several dtypes. Field access returns a normal array, so all the usual reductions apply.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

dtype = np.dtype([('name', 'U4'), ('score', 'i4')])
rows = np.array([('ada', 91)], dtype=dtype)
print(rows['score'].tolist())

debug.title: A field the dtype never declared

a = np.array([(1, 2.5)], dtype=[('id', 'i4')])
print(a['score'])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np

debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.array(['2026-13-01'], dtype='datetime64[D]'))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
print(np.array(['2026-12-01'], dtype='datetime64[D]'))

learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array(['num', 'py'])
print(np.char.upper(a))

learn.title: Fixed-width strings truncate
learn.body: A U2 dtype stores at most two characters per element, so longer text is cut on creation rather than at print time.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.array(["abcd"], dtype="U2"))

learn.title: object dtype keeps Python objects
learn.body: dtype=object stores pointers to arbitrary Python values, which is flexible but loses the fast numeric paths that make arrays worthwhile.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, "x", None], dtype=object)
print(a.dtype, a[1])

learn.title: timedelta64 tells the gap
learn.body: Subtracting two datetime64 values returns a timedelta64, so date arithmetic reports an interval in the unit of the operands.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.datetime64('2024-01-03') - np.datetime64('2024-01-01'))

learn.title: Divide a timedelta to get a count
learn.body: Dividing a timedelta64 by a unit timedelta converts it to a plain number, which is how you get days, hours or seconds for analysis.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
d = np.datetime64('2024-01-03') - np.datetime64('2024-01-01')
print(d / np.timedelta64(1, 'D'))

learn.title: Fields are read by name
learn.body: A structured array indexes its fields by name, so a price column is a plain array you can sum without unpacking the records.
learn.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([(1, 2.5), (2, 3.5)], dtype=[('id', 'i4'), ('price', 'f4')])
print(a['price'].sum())

learn.title: char functions work elementwise on text
learn.body: The `np.char` namespace applies string methods to every element without a Python loop.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.char.upper(np.array(['np', 'ai'])).tolist())

learn.title: str_len counts characters
learn.body: Length is a property of the string, not the fixed-width buffer. Padding does not inflate the count.
learn.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.char.str_len(np.array(['ab', 'cde'])).tolist())

learn.title: Datetime differences are timedeltas
learn.body: Subtracting two `datetime64` values gives a `timedelta64`, which converts to a number by dividing by a unit.

import numpy as np

start = np.datetime64('2026-01-01')
