modules.title: Masked Arrays and Numerical Robustness
modules.goal: Detect and handle NaN and infinity honestly, and choose masked arrays or nan-aware functions deliberately.

topics.title: NaN is not equal to anything
topics.body: isnan locates missing values and nanmean ignores them; plain mean propagates NaN, so one missing reading can hide the whole summary.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])
print(np.isnan(a), np.nanmean(a))

topics.title: Infinity is a value, not a missing one
topics.body: isinf finds overflow and division-by-zero results; infinity is a real float value, so it must be filtered or clipped rather than treated as missing.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.isinf(np.array([1.0, np.inf])))

topics.title: Masked arrays carry their own mask
topics.body: A masked array stores a boolean mask beside the data, and reductions ignore masked positions — cleaner than overwriting values with NaN.
topics.code:
import numpy.ma as ma
a = ma.masked_array([1, 2, 3], mask=[0, 1, 0])
print(a.mean())

topics.title: isnan builds the mask
topics.body: NaN never equals itself, so isnan is the only reliable way to locate missing values before you decide to drop or fill them.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1., np.nan])
print(np.isnan(a))

topics.title: nanmean ignores missing values
topics.body: mean propagates one NaN to the answer while nanmean skips those elements and averages the rest, so the two numbers differ on dirty data.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1., np.nan, 3.])
print(np.mean(a), np.nanmean(a))

topics.title: nan_to_num replaces NaN and infinity
topics.body: nan_to_num swaps non-finite values for finite defaults, which keeps a downstream model from receiving poisoning values.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.nan_to_num(np.array([np.nan, np.inf, -np.inf])))

topics.title: allclose can treat NaN as equal
topics.body: By default two NaNs are not close, because allclose compares with ==; equal_nan=True is the switch that makes them match.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.allclose([np.nan], [np.nan], equal_nan=True), np.allclose([np.nan], [np.nan]))

topics.title: nanargmax skips NaN
topics.body: argmax can return the position of a NaN, while nanargmax ignores them and returns the position of the largest real value.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.nanargmax([1., np.nan, 3.]))

topics.title: NaN never equals itself
topics.body: IEEE 754 defines `NaN != NaN`, so equality checks can never find missing values. Use `np.isnan` instead.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.nan == np.nan)

topics.title: isnan finds missing values
topics.body: The result is a boolean array, ready to be inverted with `~` or counted with `sum`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.isnan(np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])).tolist())

topics.title: nanstd ignores the gaps
topics.body: The `nan`-prefixed reductions skip missing values. Plain `std` would return `nan` for the whole array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(round(float(np.nanstd(np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0]))), 6))

topics.title: Mask NaN, then reduce
topics.body: Filtering with `~np.isnan(a)` is the explicit alternative to the `nan`-prefixed functions and works with any reduction.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])
print(a[~np.isnan(a)].mean())

debug.title: NaN silently wins the mean
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])
print(a.mean())
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])
print(np.nanmean(a))
debug.error: prints nan — mean() propagates NaN; use nanmean when values are missing

debug.fix:

a = np.array([1, np.nan], dtype=float)
print(np.isnan(a))

modules.title: Performance and Vectorization
modules.goal: Replace Python loops with vectorised code, reuse buffers with out= and benchmark changes honestly.

topics.title: Vectorised reduction
topics.body: One NumPy expression runs in compiled loops over contiguous memory, so a million-element sum needs no Python iteration.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(1_000_000)
print(int((a * 2).sum()))

topics.title: Reuse a buffer with out=
topics.body: Passing out= writes the result into an existing array, avoiding a new allocation in hot loops where the shape is already known.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
out = np.empty_like(a)
np.multiply(a, 2, out=out)
print(out)

topics.title: Chunk large work
topics.body: array_split lets you process a big array in bounded pieces, which keeps peak memory predictable on datasets that do not fit comfortably.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print(sum(int(chunk.sum()) for chunk in np.array_split(a, 2)))

topics.title: einsum replaces a triple loop
topics.body: einsum writes the sum over indices in the subscript string, so a dot product, a trace or a batched contraction is one compiled call.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3.)
print(np.einsum('i,i->', a, a))

topics.title: dot and @ agree
topics.body: np.dot and the @ operator compute the same matrix product, and proving it with allclose is a good habit before optimising either side.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.arange(4.).reshape(2, 2)
B = np.eye(2)
print(np.allclose(np.dot(A, B), A @ B))

topics.title: bincount counts integer categories
topics.body: bincount tallies non-negative integers in one pass, so labelled data is counted without a Python loop or a dictionary.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.bincount(np.array([0, 1, 1, 3])))

topics.title: vectorize wraps a Python function
topics.body: np.vectorize applies a scalar function elementwise for convenience, but it loops in Python underneath and is not a speed-up.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
f = np.vectorize(lambda x: x * x)
print(f(np.array([1, 2, 3])))

topics.title: sum in chunks instead of one huge temporary
topics.body: Adding slice sums keeps peak memory small, because each chunk is released instead of materialising a full-size intermediate array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print(sum(a[i:i + 4].sum() for i in range(0, 10, 4)))

topics.title: add.reduce sums along an axis
topics.body: Every ufunc has a `reduce` that applies it down an axis. It is the general form behind `sum`, `prod` and `max`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.add.reduce(np.arange(5)))

topics.title: einsum can read a diagonal
topics.body: Repeating an index in `einsum` means "same position on both axes", which extracts or sums the diagonal without a mask.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(np.einsum('ii->', A))

topics.title: bincount needs non-negative integers
topics.body: The output length is one more than the largest value, so position `i` counts how often `i` appeared. Floats raise a `TypeError`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.bincount(np.array([0, 1, 1, 3])).tolist())

topics.title: dot on matrices is a matrix product
topics.body: On two 2-D arrays, `np.dot` and `@` agree. Confusing it with elementwise `*` is the classic shape bug.
topics.code:
import numpy as np

print(np.dot(np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1]]), np.array([2, 3])).tolist())

debug.title: An out array of the wrong shape
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
out = np.empty(2)
np.add([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], out=out)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
out = np.empty(3)
np.add([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], out=out)
print(out)
debug.error: ValueError: output array is not acceptable (shape mismatch)

debug.title: In-place add on an alias
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
b = a
b += 1
print(a)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
b = a.copy()
b += 1
print(a)
debug.error: prints [1 2 3 4 5] — b was the same object, not a copy

debug.title: A dot product with mismatched inner sizes
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
b = np.ones((2, 3))
print(a @ b)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
b = np.ones((2, 3))
print(a @ b.T)
debug.error: ValueError: matmul: Input operand 1 has a mismatch in its core dimension 0, with gufunc signature (n?,k),(k,m?)->(n?,m?)

debug.title: In-place add on an alias
debug.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
b = a
b += 1
print(a)
debug.error: prints [1 2 3 4 5] — b was the same object, not a copy
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
b = a.copy()
b += 1
print(a)

debug.title: A dot product with mismatched inner sizes
debug.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
b = np.ones((2, 3))
print(a @ b)
debug.error: ValueError: matmul: Input operand 1 has a mismatch in its core dimension 0, with gufunc signature (n?,k),(k,m?)->(n?,m?)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
b = np.ones((2, 3))
print(a @ b.T)
